_note: Frozen content for design review. Branching family — one question per page, two answers, and the consequence of each. Connectors drawn as orthogonal rules, no arrows.
brief: Six decisions that quietly determine whether a project ships

slots.eyebrow: Six forks, and the one nobody notices taking
slots.subtitle: Each of these is a two-minute choice made early, and each one determines about a month of what follows.
slots.rootQuestion: Does anyone outside the team want this?
slots.cardSub1: The most expensive way to answer a question that costs an afternoon.
slots.cardSub2: One named person who asked beats a segment that might.

slots.title: Who asked for this?
slots.subtitle: The answer determines whether you are building a product or an opinion.
slots.rootQuestion: Can you name the person who asked?
slots.cardSub1: Internal ideas are not worse, they are just unvalidated and feel identical to validated ones.
slots.cardSub2: One real request is a thread you can pull. Ten guesses are not.
slots.takeawayBody: A named person beats a market size on every slide it appears on.

slots.title: Can this ship in a week?
slots.subtitle: Not whether it should, whether it could. The answer is a measurement of how much you are guessing.
slots.rootQuestion: Could a usable version ship this week?
slots.cardSub1: Long projects are not more ambitious. They defer the moment you learn you were wrong.
slots.cardTitle2: You will learn in seven days
slots.cardSub2: Whatever comes back changes the next version, which is the entire point.
slots.takeawayBody: Scope is a bet on how long you can afford to be wrong for.

slots.title: Is it blocked, or is it waiting?
slots.subtitle: These look identical on a board and need opposite responses.
slots.rootQuestion: Is somebody actively working on it?
slots.cardSub1: Most delay is queueing, not difficulty, and queueing is fixable by one message.
slots.cardSub2: Rare, and worth protecting. Adding people here makes it slower, not faster.
slots.takeawayBody: Nine times in ten a stalled task is waiting on a person, not a problem.

slots.title: Is this a feature or a symptom?
slots.subtitle: Requests describe solutions. The useful work is getting back to what went wrong.
slots.rootQuestion: Did they describe a problem or a control?
slots.cardSub1: A specific request usually means a specific frustration you have not heard yet.
slots.cardSub2: Knowing the problem leaves the solution open, which is where the leverage is.
slots.takeawayBody: Every toggle in a settings page is a conversation somebody skipped.

slots.title: Is it bad, or is it just old?
slots.subtitle: Code you did not write and do not understand feels identical to code that is genuinely wrong.
slots.rootQuestion: Has it caused a real incident?
slots.cardTitle1: It offends, it does not fail
slots.cardSub1: Rewrites trade a known set of bugs for an unknown one, on a schedule nobody believes.
slots.cardSub2: Replace the part that broke, not the system it lives in.
slots.takeawayBody: Ugly and working outlives elegant and half-finished, every time.

slots.title: Would you make this call again?
slots.subtitle: The only way any of these improve is by checking them afterwards, which almost nobody does.
slots.rootQuestion: Did you write down what you expected?
slots.cardSub1: Memory edits the prediction to match the outcome, reliably and invisibly.
slots.cardSub2: One line written in advance is the difference between experience and anecdote.
slots.takeawayBody: A decision you cannot review is a decision you will keep repeating.

slots.eyebrow: One fork, on the current project
slots.subtitle: One sentence on what you expect to happen, dated. It costs nothing and it is the only thing that turns six of these into experience.
slots.rootQuestion: Did you write down what you expected?
slots.cardSub1: Confident, unfalsifiable, and identical to everyone else's.
slots.cardSub2: Boring, checkable, and the reason the next call is better.
slots.signoff: The record is the whole method
